stories.title: From pressure to proof: Leading through constraint in the data center era
stories.summary: The article examines how data center leadership teams are adapting to operating under constraints such as limited power, talent, and capital. It highlights a mindset shift within teams as a prerequisite for turning resource pressure into demonstrable operational results.
stories.why_it_matters: Constraint is now the default operating condition for the industry, and organizations that treat scarcity as a design parameter rather than a temporary setback are better positioned to deliver. Executives and managers can draw practical lessons on culture and decision-making under sustained pressure.
stories.content:
One of the most revealing benchmarks of a leader is what their teams can produce when the conditions are stacked against them. I’ve spent my career thinking about how to inspire a team to not only persevere but thrive in those environments. Interestingly, it’s under those same conditions where our best work is produced.

There are four priorities that guide my decisions: customer, company, culture, and careers. Every day my responsibility is to recognize what is important and what can wait, when the answers aren’t obvious and the minutes are precious. Here is a story about what those priorities look like under pressure, and what a team can accomplish when the order holds.

## **From flexible to non-negotiable: The mindset shift the team needed**

A few years ago, our Data Center Solutions (DCS) business unit reached an inflection point. We had missed a critical window which, in the data center space, is a rapidly compounding problem. Massive infrastructure decisions get made without you. Ecosystems form around competitors. The window of opportunity doesn’t reopen on your schedule.

That inflection point wasn’t limited to a single business unit. About a year ago, Microchip took a hard look at itself, and we recognized that change was necessary. Years of acquisitions and organic growth had expanded the company, but they had also introduced complexity that affected how consistently we executed. Between 2008 and 2020, Microchip acquired roughly sixteen different companies. While that growth strengthened the portfolio, it also left parts of the organization fragmented, with silos, various ideals around business processes, and competing priorities slowing decision-making. Over the last year, we’ve addressed those issues directly and have worked to restructure strategy, reorganize teams, and realign the company around how we wanted to operate going forward.

This forced a reckoning. We had been treating Time-To-Market (TTM) as a variable or a “lever” to negotiate when engineering got complicated or resources ran thin. That had to end.

“Time is no longer a variable. Our customers are building billion-dollar data centers – they can’t wait for us to be ready.”

I asked my team to make a fundamental shift in how they think about deliverables. I use an analogy that tends to land quickly: you don’t get to choose when the Olympics are held. You train for the date, not when you feel ready. The moment TTM became a constant rather than a variable, the question changed. It stopped being “can we move the deadline?” and became “what do we have to solve to hit it?” Identifying the constraint of time as a catalyst for action is where the transformation began.

This is also where the Company priority came into focus. An enterprise must survive to innovate. Sometimes that means a business operates within constraints it didn’t choose or defers to a broader organizational need. That is a strategic advantage, not a concession, and it’s how I believe a healthy company operates. When I saw it in practice, I got excited because that was a core improvement that rapidly accelerated our capabilities. We were proving that Microchip’s Data Center Solutions team could execute at the highest level when it mattered the most.

## **The evolutionary bet: Precision over brute force**

Once the mindset shifted, the decisions that followed were bold, and the team knew they had to be. Developing the SwitchTec™ PCIe Gen 6 switch wasn’t an incremental movement on what came before. It was a deliberate leap to 3 nm technology, with no roadmap to follow and no precedent to lean on. Every challenge was genuinely new.

There’s an analogy I return to when I think about what made this decision right. Our ancestors evolved (in part) by choosing precision of movement over raw strength. Fine motor control was a tradeoff that defined an era. Fast-forward a few millennia, and we are learning how to collapse these tradeoffs entirely. The returns from that first bet compounded long enough that we get to make a different choice: strength AND precision, performance AND efficiency.

The results our team achieved illustrate this: Gen 6 delivered a 20 percent improvement compared to previous-generation PCIe 5.0 switches in power efficiency alongside a doubling of throughput, a combination the industry had largely accepted as a tradeoff, not a simultaneous achievement.

“The world’s most powerful data-center infrastructure also has to be the most energy efficient. Anything else isn’t sustainable.”

I want to be direct about the real driver of this decision. It wasn’t what was technically interesting, what was advancing the roadmap, it was much simpler: What do our customers need?

Data centers have become community-level infrastructure problems. Power consumption is straining grids and forcing serious policy conversations and actions. Our customers need better performance through more sustainable technology. The 3nm decision was a customer decision that happened to require extraordinary effort to execute.

## **Asking for excellence at the hardest moment**

Here is what makes this story worth telling: this happened when everything was working against it.

Resource constraints. A company navigating a broader market downturn. A team carrying the weight of a missed window. These were the conditions that I asked our team to do some of the most demanding work of their careers. I didn’t minimize it. You don’t build trust by pretending teachable moments away. You learn, and you keep going. We did just that; we felt the weight pushing inward on us, and we pushed back harder.

What made that possible was our Culture. And I have a very specific view of what a healthy culture looks like. I am a fierce competitor, externally. I always want to beat our competition and get design wins. Internally, I don’t tolerate competition between people or teams. No *Hunger Games*, no Darwinian survival dynamics. These approaches produce scar tissue, while I am interested in producing excellence.

The team that built Microchip’s SwitchTec Gen 6 PCIe switch spanned Canada, India, Malaysia, Israel, and Taiwan, and engineering centers across the United States and Europe. That kind of global collaboration can only work when people trust that if they need help, they will get it. Our CEO, Steve Sanghi, would recognize this as the Aggregate System: the idea that culture, values, and performance are one and the same.

## **The New Standard**

When you prove that performance and efficiency can improve simultaneously, you move the bar. You change what the industry is allowed to accept as “good enough.”

The conventional assumption in data center infrastructure has long been that more performance consumes more power, but that trade-off is now harder to defend. Because this was achieved, the market must adapt to it. You don’t get to claim best-in-class while accepting lower power-performance ratios. The standard has risen for everyone, us included.

When I think about what this means for the people who built it, I come back to that Career priority. The logic here is simple. You don’t have a career without solving problems for your customers, you don’t have customers without a company that can execute and you won’t stay somewhere if the culture doesn’t value you. Get the first three right, and your career has real defensible momentum. When one of our data center products wins with a board solution, roughly 30 Microchip products across every business unit ship with it. This is a win that the entire company can celebrate, and a blueprint for compounding opportunities.

## **Our Best Days Are Ahead of Us**

What began as a team under pressure has become a team that proved something. We proved what is possible when the priorities are right, and the culture remains strong.

The most advanced PCIe-based semiconductor switch built to-date, was made by people; engineers across a dozen time zones working through real difficulty toward something they believed in. A new Microchip. Our new standard. I believe that is a story worth telling, and it carries a responsibility: to stay united as an organization, and to continue raising the bar.

If you’re only designing for where the data center is today, you’re already too late. Our goal was never to win a single race. Our goal was to demonstrate, in the most demanding conditions, that Microchip belongs at the front. We’ve proven it, and now we intend to stay here.

stories.title: The fiber connectivity challenge behind AI at scale
stories.summary: CommScope specialists outline how fiber infrastructure choices affect the speed, resilience, and future flexibility of large-scale AI deployments. The discussion positions cabling architecture as a critical, often underestimated, enabler of AI networking at scale.
stories.why_it_matters: AI clusters live or die on interconnect performance, and fiber decisions made at build time are difficult and costly to reverse. Operators planning GPU-dense halls need to weigh high-count fiber, modularity, and upgrade paths now to avoid bottlenecks as bandwidth demands escalate.
stories.content:
On an architectural diagram, an AI network appears as clean lines connecting racks and switches. On the data center floor, those lines become thousands of fibers that must reach the correct GPU, work first time, and remain accessible when the system changes.

AI has raised the stakes for that physical infrastructure. Users expect immediate answers, while operators need to bring expensive compute capacity online quickly. A dirty connector, incorrectly routed fiber, or delayed delivery can prevent GPUs from joining the cluster.

Operators therefore need infrastructure that can be deployed repeatedly at scale without becoming unmanageable, while retaining enough flexibility to support new hardware.

In a recent DCD>Broadcast episode, CommScope’s Ken Hall, Scott Eischens, and Rudy Musschebroeck explore how AI is changing network design from initial installation through future expansion, and why planning for day two now matters as much as delivering day one.

## From overnight processing to immediate answers

Traditional applications could tolerate jobs running overnight. AI has created an expectation of immediacy, placing greater importance on low latency and time to first token.

“We need to enable low-latency networks so we can access data and manage the compute capabilities in a much faster, much larger environment,” says Hall. “The expectation today is immediate, or close to it.”

AI networks are built by repeating modular building blocks. GPUs and CPUs form rack-scale systems, grouped into pods and connected through layers of switching. Keeping the network flat reduces latency, but physical connectivity multiplies rapidly as clusters grow.

Musschebroeck divides that growth into three dimensions:

- **Scale-up** : Connects the GPUs and servers within a rack so they behave as one high-performance computer, today predominantly using copper.
- **Scale-out:** Links racks and pods across the data hall, largely through fiber.
- **Scale-across:** Connects separate halls, buildings, or sites when power or space constraints prevent an AI system from occupying one location.

“Every single one of those neurons needs to talk to the others,” he says, comparing the GPUs to cells in a human brain. “It’s very important that everything is tightly interconnected.”

## When clean lines become thousands of fibers

In a typical deployment, hundreds or thousands of GPUs can translate into tens of thousands of individual fiber connections. Each must be mapped, labeled, routed, and connected correctly while remaining manageable within an already crowded facility.

“When you step into a data center and see it, it’s super dense,” says Eischens. “Those nice, neat lines are a whole bunch of fiber connections going all over the place.”

For Musschebroeck, this creates three immediate deployment challenges. The first is speed: operators need materials delivered and installed quickly so substantial infrastructure investments can begin generating revenue. The second is first-time-right quality, ensuring every expected GPU appears when the system starts. The third is logistics.

“We’re looking at a 2D blueprint, but the reality is three-dimensional, with poles, different ceiling heights, and cable ladders at different heights,” he says. Cable lengths and routes must reflect the building rather than simply the network schematic.

## Taking work off the data center floor

Point-to-point cabling may appear simple, with one connection at either end, but high cable volumes can stitch cabinets together and obstruct access when equipment needs replacing or upgrading. Structured cabling introduces an additional connection point but provides greater flexibility between cabinets and pods.

It also allows more integration, inspection, and testing to take place offsite. Trunks and utilities can be installed in advance, while cabinets are assembled and tested in a controlled environment before being rolled onto the data center floor for final connection.

This is increasingly important as different trades compete for space around AI hardware. Power, liquid cooling, and connectivity all converge on GPU cabinets. Cooling hoses and large power connections increasingly occupy the rear, pushing fiber toward the front so each system can remain accessible.

CommScope’s Rapid Fiber Connect platform, explored in a recent DCD Tech Showcase, allows GPU cabinet connections to be integrated and tested offsite, then joined through fewer Mass Insert MMC connectors.

“It pushes fiber toward the same mindset as power and cooling,” says Eischens. “Drop the cabinet into place, make a couple of clicks, and the whole cabinet is ready to go.”

## Building resilience into the physical layer

AI traffic cannot be oversubscribed in the same way as conventional cloud or telecom networks. GPUs may need to communicate with any other GPU at full speed, creating non-blocking architectures in which bandwidth is preserved through each switching layer.

The links themselves can contain multiple lanes. A 400Gbps connection, for example, may consist of four 100Gbps lanes. A multiplane architecture shuffles these lanes across different switches rather than routing them all through one. If a connection fails, the network may slow down, but the entire link does not disappear. The same approach can support more GPUs without adding another switching tier and its associated latency.

That logical resilience creates physical complexity. CommScope’s Propel shuffle modules place the lane distribution inside a replaceable module while retaining standard trunks and patch cords. If requirements change or something is damaged, operators can replace the module rather than an entire shuffled cable assembly.

Connector technology is evolving too. CommScope’s FastSelfClean technology uses V-grooves instead of conventional ferrules, cleaning the fiber end faces each time the connector is inserted. Its first planned implementation, FSC144, brings 144 fibers together in one connector with insertion loss of less than 0.1dB.

“You want to connect many fibers at the same time, and you don’t want to worry about cleaning or inspection,” says Musschebroeck. “Reliability needs to go up in these systems.”

## Following fiber into the future

The boundary between equipment and network infrastructure is also beginning to shift. Co-packaged optics integrates electrical-to-optical conversion more closely with switching silicon, reducing the power consumed by pluggable transceivers and bringing fiber deeper inside switches.

Musschebroeck expects a similar transition within rack-scale systems. Their scale-up networks are currently connected predominantly through copper, but higher speeds, greater performance, and rising GPU counts are likely to increase the role of fiber.

The definition of a cabinet may change too. Eischens notes that GPU counts per system are progressing from 72 toward 144, with 576 or more under discussion for future designs. Accommodating those systems could require multiple cabinets operating as a single unit, or an enclosure approaching the size of a small room.

Operators therefore need to consider maximum capacity, materials, labor, and expansion from the beginning. They must decide what belongs offsite and what must happen on the data center floor, while enabling repairs and upgrades without wholesale recabling.

“You’ve got to be looking at where this is going and what the next step will be,” Hall concludes. “If the next step doesn’t fit inside those walls, you’ve got to look at how you add to that.”

For AI networks, getting to the first token may be the immediate goal, but reaching it efficiently depends on planning well beyond day one.

*To hear more about how fiber infrastructure is evolving for AI, watch the full DCD>Broadcast episode with Ken Hall, Scott Eischens, and Rudy Musschebroeck,* ***here***.

stories.title: Smarter planning, intelligent construction: Building sustainable data centers of the future
stories.summary: The piece argues that sustainability has moved from optional to mandatory in data center development, with growing emphasis on energy-efficient digital infrastructure. It describes sustainable facilities as those combining prudent water and power management, low-emission construction materials, and smarter planning and construction methods.
stories.why_it_matters: As regulators, customers, and investors harden their expectations, developers who embed efficiency at the planning and construction stage avoid expensive retrofits and permitting friction. The guidance is most relevant to operators in APAC markets where green building requirements and PUE disclosure rules are tightening.
stories.content:
### With growing consciousness surrounding sustainability, the data center industry is also carefully calibrating its next steps vis-a-vis developing energy-efficient digital infrastructure; “green” data centers are no longer an option, but the mandate.

A sustainable data center is a facility that incorporates prudent water and power use practices, low-emission construction materials, energy efficient cooling and waste management systems, as well as responsible computing practices and virtualization, to ensure that the overall carbon footprint of the data center remains as low and possible without adversely impacting its productivity.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Mumbai-CDC-LATEST-Banner-2026.jpg)

#### Planning a sustainable data center

Building a sustainable or “green” data center requires a different approach to the entire planning and design process.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Syed-Mohamed-Beary-300x288.jpeg)

“Sustainability cannot be treated as an add-on at the operational stage; it must be embedded from the very conception of the project,” says Syed Mohamed Beary, Founder and CMD, Bearys Group, a company that has designed, built and delivered data centers for several international data center providers in India. “Site selection is evaluated not just from connectivity and power availability perspectives, but also climate suitability, water availability, renewable energy access and environmental impact. Building orientation, thermal performance, material selection, daylight optimization, embodied carbon and future scalability are all considered together,” adds Beary who is also Chairman, Indian Green Building Council (IGBC), Bangalore Chapter.

Elisabetta Baronio, Director– ESG Program Management, Khazna Data Centers concurs. “If sustainability is treated as an ‘add-on’, you usually miss the biggest levers,” she says. “The goal is to avoid lock-in. Once core power and cooling architectures, supply chain choices, and commissioning plans are set, it’s harder and costlier to improve outcomes later.”

Beary adds, “In conventional construction, the focus is often on CAPEX and speed of delivery. In sustainable construction, lifecycle efficiency becomes equally important.”

#### Overcoming geographical challenges

While colder climates help reduce cooling resources and power consumption, these days data centers, even humongous AI factories are being built in tropical, and even arid environments. So how do developers overcome these challenges?

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Elisabetta-Baronio-Khazna-204x300.jpeg)

“The region’s heat and humidity increase cooling demand, and water scarcity makes water stewardship a priority,” admits Baronio, whose company builds data centers in the Middle East where temperatures routinely shoot past the 45℃. “Supply chains can also vary in maturity for low-carbon materials, certified waste streams, and consistent ESG data.” But Khazna chooses to focus on elements they can control, such as thermal performance, prioritizing efficient cooling strategies, and building systems that support strong energy and water management once operational. “On the construction side, we work closely with partners to standardize methods, reduce rework, and improve material efficiency.”

Similarly in a tropical country like India there are challenges pertaining to heat management, water and power availability. Beary elaborates, “Some of the major challenges include inconsistent availability of green materials, higher upfront costs for advanced sustainable technologies, limited awareness across parts of the supply chain, and infrastructure constraints such as water stress and grid dependency. In many cases, developers also face pressure to deliver projects rapidly, which can discourage long-term sustainability thinking.” But he shed light on how to persevere despite such odds, saying, “These challenges can be overcome through integrated planning and strong stakeholder alignment. Involving sustainability consultants, architects, MEP engineers, and operators together from the early design stage, significantly improves outcomes. Vendor selection also becomes critical, choosing partners who understand lifecycle performance rather than only initial cost.”

#### The decarbonization challenge

Governments across the world are gearing up to meet an ambitious goal: Net Zero by 2050. This is in line with the findings and recommendations of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). However, keeping a data center’s carbon footprint low is much harder than what one would expect.

Yet, developers are taking the bull by its horns, employing methods like using supplementary cementitious materials, recycled steel, modular construction techniques and energy-efficient mechanical systems. “Realistic goals include reducing embodied carbon in construction materials, improving energy efficiency, maximizing renewable energy adoption, optimizing cooling systems, reducing water dependency and increasing circularity in resource usage,” says Beary.

Baronio is also a fan of practical goal setting. “Practical goals include reducing embodied carbon through smarter material choices and efficient design, minimizing waste through circularity and certified diversion pathways, and designing for energy performance and upgradeability so the facility can take advantage of cleaner power as it becomes available,” she says listing elements of Khazna’s decarbonization strategy.

#### Impact of intelligent construction on operational sustainability

Operational sustainability is directly influenced by the thought that goes into construction. The quality of design and construction determines how efficiently the facility will perform throughout its life. It also helps maintain healthy PUE and WUE during the facility’s life cycle.

“Smart sensor integration and Building Management Systems incorporated during construction enable real-time monitoring and predictive optimization later. Similarly, water-efficient plumbing infrastructure, rainwater harvesting systems, treated water reuse systems and efficient drainage planning all contribute to lower WUE performance during operations,” explains Beary.

Baronio elaborates, “At the construction stage, intelligent construction links design intent to real-world performance by reducing variability and ensuring systems are installed, tested, and commissioned exactly as intended. That starts with quality control and digital oversight, so operations teams inherit a facility that performs predictably from day one.” She adds, “It also includes designing and building for maintainability and measurement: placing sensors and metering where they matter, creating accessible routes for maintenance, and ensuring control systems are tuned and validated during commissioning.”

Beary agrees. “Intelligent construction creates the foundation upon which operational efficiency becomes achievable and scalable,” he says. “For example, optimized building envelopes reduce thermal gain and cooling loads. Efficient airflow planning during construction improves cooling performance and lowers energy consumption.” A fan of modular construction, Beary also says, “Structural planning for modular expansion prevents unnecessary future demolition and material wastage.”

#### Conclusion

In the age of AI, where we are all basically playing a catch-up game, perhaps it is important to press pause… step back and look at the bigger picture – what’s the point of building something that won’t last? A well thought-through sustainable construction strategy, that comes into play even before the facility comes together on a drawing board, will go a long way in keeping it running in an environmentally friendly manner for years to come.

stories.title: Data Centres Face Maintenance Gap Amidst Critical Infrastructure Status
stories.summary: A new industry report finds only 26% of data centres have adopted fully predictive maintenance strategies, exposing a maturity gap in operational practices. The findings come as governments increasingly classify data centres as Critical National Infrastructure, which carries higher expectations for resilience and uptime.
stories.why_it_matters: Critical infrastructure designation brings regulatory scrutiny that reactive maintenance regimes may not satisfy, putting laggard operators at compliance and outage risk. Facilities teams face pressure to invest in condition monitoring and predictive tooling before standards harden into mandates.
stories.content:
### The Maintenance Maturity Gap

The research highlights that 28% of data centre managers use a preventative maintenance model, which, while an improvement over reactive methods, still relies on fixed schedules rather than real-time equipment condition monitoring. Predictive maintenance, often supported by condition-based monitoring (CBM), continuously analyses data from critical assets like pumps, motors, and cooling systems to identify potential issues before failures occur. This approach can help reduce outages, extend equipment lifespans, and improve energy efficiency.Confidence levels among operators reflect this gap, with only 53% of respondents expressing full confidence in their current maintenance strategies. The consequences of these shortcomings are already apparent, as data centres experienced an average of six hours of unplanned downtime over the past year. Nearly nine in ten respondents (88%) reported more than three hours of downtime, and over half (52%) experienced more than six hours.

### Addressing Challenges and Moving Forward

Despite the challenges, momentum for change is building. Among organisations without a predictive maintenance strategy, 87% intend to implement one within the next six months. However, the adoption of predictive maintenance is hindered by skills shortages and a lack of specialist expertise, mirroring broader workforce capability and recruitment pressures across the sector.Implementing predictive maintenance effectively requires not just technology but also the necessary skills, processes, and organisational support to ensure measurable value. As data centres continue to underpin digital economies, maintenance is increasingly viewed as a strategic enabler of long-term success rather than a routine operational function. Closing this maintenance maturity gap is crucial for modern data centres to meet increasingly demanding standards for intelligence, foresight, and reliability.

stories.title: AI Data Centers Drive Global Semiconductor Revenue to $1.56 Trillion by 2026
stories.summary: Gartner's projection attributes the semiconductor revenue milestone to aggressive AI data center buildouts and a sharp rise in memory demand. The analysis flags that Indian hyperscalers and enterprise data center operators will face notably higher procurement costs as they expand domestic computing capacity.
stories.why_it_matters: Rising chip and memory prices flow directly into the capital budgets of data center builders, squeezing margins and potentially delaying projects in cost-sensitive markets like India. Procurement and finance teams across APAC should plan for sustained component inflation rather than waiting for a near-term correction.
stories.content:
Global semiconductor revenue is projected to reach USD 1.56 trillion in 2026, driven by aggressive AI data center construction and a significant surge in memory demand, according to Gartner. This growth is expected to notably increase procurement costs for Indian hyperscalers and enterprise data centers expanding local computing capacity.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

Global semiconductor revenue is forecast to reach USD 1.56 trillion by 2026, a 92% increase from 2025.

AI data center construction will drive 36.5% of global semiconductor revenue in 2026, over 53% by 2030.

Memory revenue is projected to exceed USD 1 trillion by 2027, with DRAM up 246.6% and NAND up 371.9% in 2026.

Rising memory prices could increase procurement costs for Indian hyperscalers and enterprise data centers.

The surge underscores the strategic importance of India's domestic semiconductor capabilities.

Global semiconductor revenue is forecast to nearly double to USD 1.56 trillion by 2026, primarily propelled by substantial investments in artificial intelligence (AI) data center infrastructure and a stronger-than-anticipated memory pricing cycle, Gartner reported on August 24.The research firm projects the market will continue its upward trajectory, reaching USD 1.94 trillion by 2027. This expansion, representing an annual increase of approximately USD 746 billion from 2025's USD 809 billion, marks a fundamental new phase of growth for the semiconductor industry, according to Gartner Director Analyst Ben Lee.

AI Infrastructure Redefines Value

The AI data center ecosystem is poised to significantly reshape value capture within the semiconductor industry. Gartner predicts that this segment will account for 36.5% of global semiconductor revenue in 2026, a figure expected to exceed 53% by 2030.Memory components are the primary catalyst for this growth. Gartner forecasts memory revenue to hit USD 837 billion in 2026 and surpass USD 1 trillion in 2027. Demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and increasing memory capacity per AI server are anticipated to elevate memory's share of total semiconductor revenue to 54% in 2026, up from 27% in 2025. Dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) revenue is expected to surge by 246.6% in 2026, while NAND flash revenue is projected to increase by 371.9%.Shrish Pant, Director Analyst at Gartner, noted that AI infrastructure has fundamentally altered the dynamics of the memory market, with continued deployment, higher server memory capacity, and sustained HBM demand driving growth through 2027 and beyond.

Broader Chip Market Expansion

Growth is not limited to memory. Non-memory semiconductor revenue is projected to increase by 21.9%, from USD 589 billion in 2025 to USD 718 billion in 2026. This demand spans central processing units (CPUs), networking silicon, power-management chips, analogue devices, and optical interconnects, all essential for supporting increasingly large AI clusters. The expansion thus extends beyond graphics processing units (GPUs) and memory, requiring investment across the broader semiconductor infrastructure stack.

Implications for Indian Data Centers

Tight global supply-demand conditions and rising memory prices are likely to increase the cost of procuring servers and other infrastructure components. Indian hyperscalers, cloud providers, and enterprise data centers planning to expand local computing capacity could face higher capital costs per rack. This is an inference from Gartner's global forecast, as the research firm did not provide India-specific projections. Enterprise technology leaders may need to factor potential procurement constraints and higher component costs into their infrastructure expansion plans through 2027.The global surge in semiconductor demand also reinforces the strategic importance of India's efforts to develop domestic semiconductor manufacturing capabilities. Chip-design companies, fabrication facilities, and semiconductor assembly and testing operations could benefit from sustained global demand across categories such as power-management chips and analogue silicon.

stories.title: AWS, Nvidia to Deploy 2 Million More GPUs for AI Workloads
stories.summary: The expanded AWS-NVIDIA agreement covers not only GPU deployment but also collaboration across CPUs, networking, and robotics, broadening the scope of the two companies' infrastructure partnership. The additional 2 million GPUs will be dedicated to AI workloads, marking one of the largest single commitments to AI compute capacity to date.
stories.why_it_matters: This deal tightens the coupling between the dominant cloud provider and the dominant AI chip supplier, raising the bar for rivals seeking GPU supply at scale. For APAC operators and enterprises, it signals that hyperscale AI capacity will keep concentrating within the largest clouds, shaping pricing, availability, and colocation demand across the region.
stories.content:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) and NVIDIA plan to deploy 2 million additional graphics processing units (GPUs) for artificial intelligence (AI) workloads. This expansion extends their collaboration to central processing units (CPUs), networking, and robotics, significantly scaling AI compute infrastructure.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

AWS and NVIDIA to deploy 2 million additional GPUs for AI workloads.

Collaboration expands to include CPUs, networking, and robotics.

Deployment scales infrastructure for surging AI computing demand.

NVIDIA remains dominant in AI chips; AWS balances with in-house silicon.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) and NVIDIA are set to deploy an additional 2 million graphics processing units (GPUs) dedicated to artificial intelligence (AI) workloads, further intensifying the race to build out AI computing capacity. The expanded collaboration will also extend into central processing units (CPUs), networking, and robotics, signalling a broader infrastructure focus.The deployment will augment NVIDIA hardware already operating across AWS's cloud platform. NVIDIA holds a dominant position in AI chip supply, while AWS manages demand for NVIDIA systems alongside its own in-house silicon, including Trainium and Inferentia.

Broader Infrastructure Build-Out

The expanded partnership indicates a relationship moving beyond just graphics processors. By including CPUs, networking, and robotics, the companies are working across a wider range of technologies crucial for data centre expansion and AI system design. Cloud infrastructure groups are heavily investing in processors, networking equipment, and power to support the growing use of generative AI services.NVIDIA's chips remain central to this build-out, widely used for training large language models and running inference tasks. For AWS, these additional GPUs can help serve customers who prefer accessing NVIDIA systems through the cloud rather than establishing their own data centre infrastructure. This arrangement also reflects how large cloud operators aim to maintain flexibility by combining merchant chip supply with internally developed processors and integrated networking gear.Robotics represents a newer area of collaboration. NVIDIA has developed software and hardware platforms for robotic systems and industrial automation, while Amazon has long invested in warehouse automation and machine learning systems for its logistics network. Deeper collaboration in this segment suggests the partnership could extend beyond cloud computing into physical AI applications.

Competitive Landscape and Investment

The announcement comes amidst intensifying competition among hyperscale cloud providers to secure necessary equipment for AI services. Companies like Microsoft and Google are expanding their infrastructure, signing supply agreements, and introducing proprietary chip designs to manage costs and reduce reliance on external vendors. This competitive environment underscores NVIDIA's strategic importance to major technology groups.Even as customers explore alternatives, NVIDIA's GPUs and networking products are deeply embedded in current AI system architectures, making access to supply a priority for cloud operators serving startups, developers, and large corporate clients. The inclusion of CPUs in the alliance highlights closer alignment in AI system assembly, as CPUs remain essential for orchestrating workloads, managing memory, and running broader application environments within data centres.Networking has also become critical as AI clusters grow larger, with rapid data movement between processors being vital for efficient model training. NVIDIA has expanded its presence in this segment through high-speed interconnect and data centre networking products. Closer collaboration with AWS on networking could influence the configuration of future AI clusters within the cloud provider's infrastructure.The scale of 2 million additional GPUs underscores the capital-intensive nature of AI infrastructure development among major technology companies. Building and operating such systems requires significant investment in chips, servers, networking, software integration, cooling, and electricity. Investors and customers are monitoring whether this AI infrastructure spending will translate into sustainable revenue growth for cloud providers and semiconductor firms. AWS faces pressure to demonstrate that AI service demand can support rapid expansion costs, while NVIDIA addresses questions about the sustainability of current demand levels. This deployment, however, indicates both companies are preparing for continued AI growth across various sectors.

stories.title: AI Rack Density Limits: Power, Cooling, Failure Risk
stories.summary: Rapidly climbing AI rack densities are overwhelming conventional air cooling and legacy power distribution architectures in existing facilities. Operators are being pushed toward liquid cooling, higher-voltage DC power delivery, and more sophisticated failure detection to keep high-density deployments stable.
stories.why_it_matters: Facilities designed for traditional enterprise loads cannot host modern AI hardware without deep retrofit work, forcing operators to choose between costly upgrades and stranded capacity. The shift reshapes site selection, commissioning timelines, and the skill sets required of operations staff.
stories.content:
### Cooling and Power Delivery Challenges

The primary limits to rack density are how much heat a rack can remove, the power drawn by the chips, and the facility’s ability to safely deliver that power. Joseph Wolff, founder and CTO of eRacks Systems, highlighted that the misconception is that density is capped by GPU count or easily fixed with bigger fans. Air cooling becomes impractical above approximately 50 kW per rack, as fans cannot move enough air to manage the thermal load, according to Uptime Institute.Liquid cooling has emerged as the standard solution. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling, which delivers coolant through cold plates on the chip, handles 100 to 150 kW per rack and accounted for 55% market share in 2026, as per Schneider Electric. Two-phase immersion cooling, previously hindered by PFAS restrictions, is recovering with a replacement fluid qualified in early 2026. Microsoft and Swiss startup Corintis reported in September 2025 that microchannels etched directly into a chip could remove heat up to three times more effectively than standard cold plates in lab tests.Power delivery presents an equally critical constraint. Omkar Nimbalkar, vice president of multi-vendor support services at IBM, noted that density is bounded by electrical engineering and failure planning, not just chip specifications. Legacy 54 VDC power distribution faces a hard limit above roughly 200 kW per rack due to the impracticality of the required copper cabling. Furthermore, redundancy requirements impose a capacity tax; a typical power distribution unit (PDU) handles about 20 kW in a double-redundant configuration.

### Emerging Solutions and Future Outlook

Several solutions are moving from pilot phases to standard deployment. Higher-voltage DC distribution, such as the 800 VDC used in Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72, is gaining traction, with commercial offerings from Vertiv, Schneider Electric, Eaton, and Delta slated for late 2026. Foxconn’s 40 MW Kaohsiung-1 facility in Taiwan is being built with 800 VDC. The Open Compute Project’s Mount Diablo initiative, which reached its 0.7.0 specification in March 2026, aims to disaggregate power delivery from compute racks, allowing independent scaling.On-site and behind-the-meter generation are also becoming more prevalent for mega-scale AI campuses, driven by constraints in grid power availability. Christopher Miglino, CEO of Axe Compute, stressed that the critical factor is not just campus-level megawatts on paper, but the power that can be reliably delivered, cooled, and operated to a single rack.As rack densities increase, the cost of single failures also rises, necessitating advanced firmware-level failure detection to throttle racks down in seconds. Nimbalkar expects that by 2028, typical high-density AI racks will likely exceed 100 kW, featuring direct liquid cooling, 400 V power delivery, and integrated failure-handling logic. Wolff anticipates a bifurcation, with most enterprises retaining air-cooled systems while a smaller segment pushes far beyond 100 kW.

### India Outlook

India's data center operators and hyperscalers deploying AI infrastructure will face these power and cooling challenges directly. This necessitates the rapid adoption of advanced liquid cooling and higher-voltage DC distribution to support next-generation AI compute. The growing need for on-site power generation could also accelerate distributed energy solutions for AI campuses across India, helping to bypass existing grid limitations. Indian data center design and construction firms will need to quickly integrate these new architectural and engineering requirements to remain competitive in the evolving AI infrastructure landscape. The shift will require substantial capital expenditure and a re-evaluation of existing facility designs to ensure resilience and scalability for future AI workloads.

stories.title: Blue Owl leads $3.4b Iren debt deal to buy Nvidia's chips
stories.summary: Investment firm Blue Owl is leading a $3.4 billion debt financing package for cloud provider Iren, with proceeds earmarked for purchasing Nvidia chips. The deal underscores the growing role of private credit in funding AI compute acquisitions.
stories.why_it_matters: Private credit stepping in to fund GPU purchases shows how capital markets are adapting to finance the AI infrastructure boom beyond traditional bank lending. It also lowers the barrier for mid-tier operators to acquire high-end silicon, intensifying competition for capacity and power.
stories.content:
Olivia Fishlow

Blue Owl Capital funds led a $US2.4 billion ($3.4 billion) debt deal for cloud computing provider Iren, which will use the proceeds to buy Nvidia’s Blackwell Ultra GPUs for a data centre campus in Canada.

The deal consists of a US$ 1.2 billion senior-secured term loan and an equal amount of senior-secured notes, and is structured to allow the Sydney-based Iren to purchase equipment in stages over a defined period.
